title: Dedicated capacity deep dive: provisioning lead times + readiness validation
topics: Dedicated capacity provisioning workflow and typical lead times
Readiness gates: GPU health, networking/DNS/TLS, runtime smoke tests
Perf-canary readiness benchmark and acceptance thresholds
Rollout expectations: staged enablement, manual overrides, and rollback points
Auditability: change logs, break-glass overrides, and image provenance
summary: HelioBank asked for a concrete breakdown of Redwood Dedicated provisioning lead time (request → Ready) and what validation is performed before capacity is allowed into routing. Redwood walked through the pipeline stages (provisioning, imaging, bootstrap, validation), clarified Ready semantics (routing only uses Ready), and reviewed readiness gates including a lightweight perf-canary run. HelioBank emphasized change-management and audit requirements (who approved, what changed, evidence of checks) and requested sample artifacts (dashboard screenshots, readiness JSON output, and runbook excerpts). Next steps include sharing a stage budget / SLO proposal, a sample readiness report, and scheduling a short follow-up focused on security controls and operational handoff.
action_items: Lauren Bishop - Send HelioBank a one-page 'time-to-ready' stage breakdown with p50/p95 targets and what is included/excluded - Due 2025-02-21
Vanessa Ortiz - Provide an example of the provisioning state timeline (stage start/finish events) and what operators see when a stage fails - Due 2025-02-21
Rafael Mendes - Share proposed alerting/paging thresholds for stuck stages + what triggers a ticket vs page - Due 2025-02-26
Rina Kobayashi - Send sample perf-canary readiness output (pass/fail JSON + summary) and the default thresholds used for 'Ready' - Due 2025-02-26
Marcus Lin - Confirm what evidence Redwood can provide for image provenance (signing/attestation) and audit logs for break-glass overrides - Due 2025-02-28
Samir Patel - Confirm HelioBank’s target region(s), initial GPU SKU preferences, and any maintenance window constraints for the pilot bring-up - Due 2025-02-23
Carlos Renteria - Provide HelioBank’s required change-management artifacts (CAB approval format, audit retention expectations) so Redwood can map to existing logs - Due 2025-02-23
next_steps: Redwood to share a provisioning/readiness 'evidence pack' (sample dashboard view + readiness report) for HelioBank’s internal review.
Schedule a 30-minute security/ops follow-up to align on audit logs, break-glass controls, and access boundaries.
If HelioBank agrees on Ready criteria, Redwood to propose a pilot plan: staging pool first, then a production expansion window with explicit rollback points.
transcript:
Meeting: Dedicated capacity deep dive: provisioning lead times + readiness validation
Meeting ID: ff_8d21c1a4
Recorded: 2025-02-19 17:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Lauren Bishop, Vanessa Ortiz, Rafael Mendes, Rina Kobayashi, Marcus Lin
HelioBank: Samir Patel, Megan Chu, Carlos Renteria, Anika Wolff

---

[00:00] Lauren Bishop: Alright, I think we’re good. Thanks everyone for making the time. The goal today is, um, less “product overview” and more a technical deep dive on Dedicated provisioning lead times and what we mean by “ready” before routing uses anything.

[00:14] Samir Patel: Yep. That’s exactly it. We’re getting a lot of pressure internally on predictable timelines. Like, if we ask for 64 more GPUs, what does that mean in days and what are the gates.

[00:27] Lauren Bishop: Got it. Maybe quick intros and then we’ll jump straight into the lifecycle.

[00:31] Vanessa Ortiz: Vanessa, I run the fleet automation workstream on our side.

[00:35] Rafael Mendes: Rafael, SRE lead for readiness gates and rollout safety.

[00:38] Rina Kobayashi: Rina, I own perf-canary integration, so the benchmark you’ll hear about.

[00:43] Marcus Lin: Marcus, security engineering approver for images and audit trails.

[00:47] Samir Patel: Samir, platform eng.

[00:49] Megan Chu: Megan, SRE, I’ll be the one getting paged if this goes sideways.

[00:52] Carlos Renteria: Carlos, security architect.

[00:55] Anika Wolff: Anika, vendor management and procurement.

[01:00] Lauren Bishop: Cool. Samir, do you want to frame the exact question so we can anchor?

[01:06] Samir Patel: Sure. We’re comparing Dedicated offerings—some folks are pushing us to just do AWS Bedrock or Azure OpenAI. The appeal there is “you don’t manage capacity.” But we need predictable performance and some data isolation. So if we do Dedicated with you: what’s the end-to-end workflow from request to traffic, what’s the lead time, and what’s the proof that it’s healthy before it takes prod traffic.

[01:31] Lauren Bishop: Perfect. So we usually talk about it as “provision-to-ready.” Vanessa can walk the stages, and Rafael can cover the gates and the semantics.

[01:41] Vanessa Ortiz: Yep. So, high level: we have a requested pool expansion, then we provision infra (networking + compute), then imaging (golden image on GPU nodes), then cluster bootstrap (k8s components, runtime chart), then validation (smoke tests + GPU checks + perf-canary), and only then do we mark it Ready in the control plane.

[02:05] Megan Chu: And “Ready” means it can take traffic automatically?

[02:08] Rafael Mendes: Correct, with an important detail: routing only advertises capacity that is in Ready. Anything in Validating is explicitly not used. We made that a hard boundary because previously teams got burned by “mostly up” capacity.

[02:21] Samir Patel: Okay. Can you quantify each stage? Like, where the time goes.

[02:26] Vanessa Ortiz: That depends on region and SKU, but I can give you typical and worst-case drivers. Provisioning the infra itself, when quota is available and the module applies cleanly, is often ~30–60 minutes. Imaging can be 20–40 minutes per node, but parallelized. Bootstrap is usually 15–30. Validation is 10–20 minutes. The big spikes are quotas and imaging artifact downloads.

[02:55] Anika Wolff: When you say quota, do you mean you’re waiting on cloud capacity? Like availability of GPUs?

[03:01] Vanessa Ortiz: Yeah, exactly. If we’re in a constrained region or a specific GPU type is tight, that’s not a software pipeline issue. But for the software part, we’re trying to reduce variability and make it deterministic.

[03:15] Samir Patel: Our biggest issue in prior vendors is “we think it’s up,” then we run real load and it’s like, no, performance is half what you expected. That’s the readiness proof part.

[03:27] Rina Kobayashi: Yeah, that’s why we added perf-canary as a gate. It’s not a full benchmark suite—because you don’t want a 4-hour run—but it exercises the end-to-end serving path with a small set of prompts and measures tokens/sec and p95 latency. It produces a pass/fail plus a JSON summary.

[03:49] Megan Chu: What exactly is it measuring? Like per-GPU throughput? Or the whole pool?

[03:54] Rina Kobayashi: Whole pool, but it tags results per node as well. The “readiness suite” runs a few fixed concurrency levels. It’s meant to catch obvious regressions: wrong driver, wrong runtime build, misconfigured batching, network egress issues, that type of thing.

[04:13] Carlos Renteria: Is that report stored somewhere for audit? Like can you show us “this pool passed on date X.”

[04:19] Rafael Mendes: Yes. The intent is each provisioning run has a correlation ID; we emit stage start/finish/failure events, and we attach artifacts links—logs, and the perf-canary JSON. For audit you can see “who triggered, what config version, what image version, and what checks ran.”

[04:39] Samir Patel: Who triggers it? That’s important. We need change-management. Like we can’t have random people kicking off capacity changes.

[04:47] Vanessa Ortiz: Right now it’s operator-triggered, but RBAC’d. Only the fleet/provisioning role can trigger. There’s also a pause/resume so you can stop mid-flight. And we have a break-glass override for config validation, but that’s admin-only with audit logs.

[05:06] Carlos Renteria: “Break-glass” makes me nervous. What does that actually bypass.

[05:10] Marcus Lin: It bypasses specific policy gates in config validation—like if a customer has an edge-case network CIDR that our linter flags incorrectly. When break-glass is used, we log an audit entry with actor, timestamp, justification string, and we alert internally. It’s not silent.

[05:30] Megan Chu: Also, can you define the config? Like what is being validated.

[05:34] Vanessa Ortiz: Pool config includes region, SKU, node count, some helm values for the runtime, network settings, and policy flags like allowed egress. Validation checks for known footguns—bad CIDR ranges, conflicting autoscaling settings, missing TLS cert references, invalid runtime flags. It’s basically “don’t let us shoot ourselves in the foot.”

[05:58] Samir Patel: Okay. Let’s talk lead times as commitments. If we sign something, what do you actually commit to?

[06:05] Lauren Bishop: Great question. There’s a difference between “capacity procurement/availability” and “time-to-ready once capacity is allocated.” We’re working toward an SLO for the automation portion. For example: X percent of expansions are Ready within Y hours once we have GPUs assigned. But we won’t promise GPU availability in a constrained region without a reservation.

[06:30] Anika Wolff: That’s aligned with how we purchase, yes.

[06:33] Samir Patel: We’d want it written clearly. Like what you can control.

[06:37] Lauren Bishop: Yep. We can share a stage budget and an SLO proposal after this.

[06:44] Megan Chu: Also, what happens when it fails. Like, does it keep retrying forever and we find out at 2am?

[06:51] Rafael Mendes: No. Each stage has bounded retries with backoff. If you hit a failure state, it’s explicit: Failed with an error category. And we post status updates in our #eng-infra channel and open a ticket for non-paging issues. Paging thresholds are for “stuck” stages beyond a time window or repeated failures.

[07:14] Megan Chu: What are the time windows.

[07:16] Rafael Mendes: We’re tuning them, but conceptually: provisioning stuck beyond, say, 90 minutes is suspicious; imaging beyond a certain percentile in that region might page the owning team; validation stuck is usually a hard fail because it’s deterministic.

[07:35] Samir Patel: “Deterministic” is optimistic.

[07:37] Rafael Mendes: Fair. More deterministic than “terraform apply in a weird state.” But yes, we still categorize.

[07:45] Vanessa Ortiz: The important part is the run has a state machine: Requested → Provisioning → Imaging → Bootstrapping → Validating → Ready, or Failed. Each transition is persisted and audited.

[08:01] Samir Patel: Okay. Can you walk through an example? Like we ask Monday morning for an expansion. What happens.

[08:08] Vanessa Ortiz: Sure. Monday 9am you request an expansion for, say, us-east, 32 H100s. We create a provisioning run with an ID. First we run an IaC apply for network + compute. Output is a set of node IDs and cluster endpoint. Then imaging: nodes pull the golden image version “gpu-node-2025.02.14” or whatever. Then bootstrap: we install baseline k8s add-ons and the Redwood runtime chart pinned to a version. Then validation: GPU health checks (including ECC error screening), DNS/TLS checks, runtime smoke tests (basic generate requests), then perf-canary. If all pass, control plane marks pool Ready and routing starts seeing it.

[08:56] Megan Chu: ECC error screening meaning you run nvidia-smi and look for errors?

[09:00] Vanessa Ortiz: Exactly. Plus we run a small CUDA sanity check. If a node has ECC errors, we mark it as unhealthy and it will be replaced before Ready.

[09:12] Samir Patel: Replacement adds time though.

[09:14] Rafael Mendes: It does, but it prevents you from taking a flaky node into production. We’d rather extend time-to-ready than violate readiness criteria.

[09:26] Samir Patel: That’s good in principle, but we need predictability.

[09:30] Lauren Bishop: Predictability plus transparency. If replacement happens, you’ll see it and you’ll see why.

[09:37] Carlos Renteria: On the image: do you sign it? And how do you manage updates. We’ve had vendors do “silent updates” and it’s a nightmare.

[09:47] Marcus Lin: We do versioned golden images. The roadmap and what we’re implementing is: build pipeline produces an artifact, it’s signed/attested, and promotion from staging to prod is explicit. We can provide the image version in the readiness evidence and in audit logs. No silent “latest” tags.

[10:09] Carlos Renteria: And if there’s a critical CVE.

[10:12] Marcus Lin: Then we build a new image version and roll it via a controlled process. For Dedicated pools, we’d coordinate a maintenance window. That’s part of the change-management story.

[10:24] Anika Wolff: Does that affect pricing or contract? Like do we pay for the downtime.

[10:28] Lauren Bishop: We can cover in commercial terms separately; today we’re focusing on the technical lifecycle, but yes, maintenance windows are planned.

[10:39] Samir Patel: Back to readiness: what’s the acceptance threshold in perf-canary. Is it like “must hit 90% of benchmark.”

[10:46] Rina Kobayashi: It’s not compared to a public benchmark; it’s compared to an expected band for that model + hardware class. Like if we deploy Llama 70B on H100, we know the typical tokens/sec at a given concurrency with our standard runtime config. If you are significantly below that, we fail.

[11:08] Samir Patel: “Significantly” is subjective.

[11:10] Rina Kobayashi: Totally. Today we use explicit thresholds—like min throughput, max p95 latency. We can share the defaults and we can tune per customer if your workload is different, but we don’t want to tune away real problems.

[11:29] Megan Chu: Could a noisy neighbor type issue cause it to fail.

[11:33] Vanessa Ortiz: On Dedicated pools you don’t have tenant sharing at the GPU layer. But you can still have cloud-level issues: network jitter, storage. The canary would catch it, but diagnosing might take some time.

[11:48] Samir Patel: That’s what we want caught.

[11:51] Lauren Bishop: Right. And again, we don’t flip to Ready until it’s within the band.

[12:00] Megan Chu: You keep saying “routing won’t use it.” Is that enforced? Like hard-coded?

[12:05] Rafael Mendes: Yes. Routing consumes the control plane Ready flag. We explicitly do not advertise anything else. There was internal debate about using “Validating” capacity for warmup traffic, but we decided no. Only Ready.

[12:23] Samir Patel: Good. We got bit by that with Together AI once—like they said it’s live but it was still initializing, and we had 5xx.

[12:32] Lauren Bishop: We’ve heard similar stories. That’s why we’re strict.

[12:37] Carlos Renteria: Who has access to the control plane. Can our people see status.

[12:41] Lauren Bishop: For Dedicated customers, you can see pool status in the console and via API. For some fields we’ll expose stage-level status. We don’t expose all internal logs by default, but we can provide a readiness report and on request share relevant logs.

[13:01] Megan Chu: I’d want at least the stage plus error category. “Failed” without why is useless.

[13:06] Rafael Mendes: Agreed. We’re improving operator-facing errors: DNS/TLS issues, GPU health, quota, helm values, etc. You’ll see “Validation failed: TLS handshake to control plane endpoint” versus “something broke.”

[13:25] Samir Patel: Helm values. You mentioned that earlier. That’s like the configuration for the runtime deployment?

[13:30] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes. Bootstrapping includes installing charts with pinned versions. Misconfigured values are a common failure mode, which is why config validation exists.

[13:42] Samir Patel: How do you prevent drift. Like if someone changes a value after readiness.

[13:47] Vanessa Ortiz: We do drift detection: compare desired config vs observed settings in the cluster/runtime. If drift is detected, it shows up as a flag in control plane and in the dashboard.

[14:02] Megan Chu: Does it auto-remediate.

[14:04] Vanessa Ortiz: Not automatically today; it surfaces it and operators investigate. Auto-remediation is risky.

[14:12] Samir Patel: Okay. Let’s talk about rollout expectations. If we do a pilot, what does it look like.

[14:18] Lauren Bishop: Generally: we start with an internal/staging pool to prove the automation and the readiness gates, then do a production expansion in a planned window. We do a staged rollout with a feature flag. There are clear rollback points: you can stop before Ready, or if Ready is marked and we see issues, we can pull it out of routing immediately.

[14:42] Megan Chu: Pull out of routing means… you can set it NotReady.

[14:45] Rafael Mendes: Correct. There’s a state transition and routing stops advertising it. That’s an emergency lever.

[14:54] Samir Patel: Is there a chance of “Ready is set too early.” I’ve seen state machines where you mark ready, then you run a test.

[15:01] Vanessa Ortiz: We had exactly that class of issue in early pilots internally, and we fixed it: Ready is only set transactionally after perf-canary completion. No “optimistic ready.”

[15:14] Megan Chu: Good. I appreciate the honesty.

[15:18] Carlos Renteria: On audit logs: we need to show who approved what. Can you integrate with our SSO.

[15:24] Lauren Bishop: We support SSO/SAML for the console for enterprise customers. For provisioning actions, those are internal operators, but we can provide audit exports. If you need customer-driven triggers, that’s a bigger conversation—we’re not offering a full self-serve provisioning UI right now.

[15:46] Samir Patel: We don’t need self-serve, but we need traceability.

[15:50] Marcus Lin: That’s consistent: each action has an actor and reason. Break-glass requires justification.

[15:59] Anika Wolff: And where is data stored. Like the logs and canary results. Data residency.

[16:05] Rafael Mendes: Logs are in our standard observability stack, region-aware. For Dedicated, we can discuss retention and residency requirements. The canary JSON is small; we can store it alongside the run metadata in the control plane and optionally export.

[16:26] Samir Patel: I want to dig into the “time-to-ready” metric. Do you track it historically.

[16:32] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes. We track overall and per-stage histograms, and we can break down by region and GPU SKU. That’s how we set stage budgets.

[16:44] Megan Chu: Can we see p95s.

[16:47] Vanessa Ortiz: We can provide reporting, yes. We don’t expose raw internal dashboards publicly today, but we can share screenshots and summary reports, and we can build customer-facing views if needed.

[17:02] Samir Patel: Okay, a concern: for regulated environments, we need minimal manual steps. Humans cause variance and audit headaches.

[17:10] Lauren Bishop: That’s the whole reason for the automation sprint we’re running. We want the workflow to be standard and repeatable with minimal handoffs.

[17:20] Megan Chu: What’s still manual today.

[17:22] Vanessa Ortiz: If quota isn’t available, there’s manual coordination. Also, some region-specific networking exceptions can require review. But the pipeline itself is automated, with manual override only if something is blocked.

[17:41] Samir Patel: And the “manual override” is the pause/resume.

[17:44] Vanessa Ortiz: Pause/resume, stage re-run (like rerun validation without re-provisioning), and break-glass for config validation—again, audited.

[17:58] Carlos Renteria: Stage re-run could be abused.

[18:01] Rafael Mendes: It’s RBAC’d. And each re-run is an event with a new run ID or a new attempt counter. You can’t hide it.

[18:14] Samir Patel: Switching topics: we also care about capacity expansion without downtime. Does adding nodes impact existing traffic.

[18:22] Rafael Mendes: Adding nodes should not impact existing nodes because it’s separate. The main risk is if a misconfiguration is applied globally. That’s why we pin runtime versions and isolate changes.

[18:38] Vanessa Ortiz: Also, in the control plane, we treat a pool expansion as adding a new slice of capacity that only joins routing once Ready. Existing slice keeps running.

[18:51] Megan Chu: That’s the “no 5xx during validation window” requirement.

[18:54] Lauren Bishop: Exactly.

[18:58] Samir Patel: Can you confirm you’re not doing “in-place upgrade” of the runtime when expanding.

[19:03] Vanessa Ortiz: Correct by default. Expansion uses the pinned version. If you want to upgrade, that’s a separate rollout with canary and rollback.

[19:15] Samir Patel: Good.

[19:18] Rina Kobayashi: Also worth noting: perf-canary readiness suite is designed to be lightweight so it doesn’t hold up expansions. We’re not trying to run your entire eval set during bring-up.

[19:34] Megan Chu: We still would run our own tests before sending customer traffic.

[19:38] Lauren Bishop: We encourage it. Our gate is the minimum bar for safety. You can add additional customer-specific acceptance checks.

[19:50] Samir Patel: If we run our own tests, do we get a pre-ready endpoint.

[19:54] Lauren Bishop: We can provide a staging route or a way to hit the pool directly without adding it to general routing, yes, depending on architecture. But the default is: until Ready, it’s not part of production routing.

[20:13] Carlos Renteria: On secrets: bootstrap requires pulling certs or tokens. How is that handled.

[20:19] Marcus Lin: Secrets are managed via our secrets management integration. Nodes don’t have long-lived creds baked in. Bootstrap uses short-lived tokens. We can talk more in the security follow-up.

[20:34] Carlos Renteria: Okay.

[20:36] Samir Patel: One more thing: you mentioned dedicated GPU pools. Do you support multiple regions with the same customer.

[20:43] Lauren Bishop: Yes. Dedicated can be multi-region. Provisioning pipeline supports multiple regions and heterogeneous SKUs, that’s a design constraint. Time-to-ready may vary by region.

[20:59] Megan Chu: Heterogeneous SKUs meaning we could have H100 in one region, A100 in another.

[21:03] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes. And the pipeline shouldn’t assume one SKU.

[21:09] Samir Patel: Alright. Let’s do some Q&A rapid fire.

[21:13] Lauren Bishop: Go for it.

[21:15] Samir Patel: 1) Can you commit to a lead time in hours for expansion.

[21:20] Lauren Bishop: For the automation portion once capacity is allocated, we can target an SLO (we’re finalizing numbers). For end-to-end including procurement, it depends.

[21:30] Samir Patel: 2) What are the explicit readiness gates.

[21:34] Rafael Mendes: GPU health (ECC, driver sanity), networking (DNS, egress, TLS handshake), runtime smoke test (basic inference request), perf-canary (throughput/latency band), plus control plane registration.

[21:52] Samir Patel: 3) Evidence: can you export a report.

[21:56] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes, we can provide a run summary including stage timings and artifacts. Rina can share a sample JSON.

[22:05] Samir Patel: 4) Rollback: if perf-canary fails.

[22:09] Vanessa Ortiz: The pool stays NotReady; we either fix and rerun stages or replace nodes. No traffic.

[22:18] Megan Chu: 5) If Ready is set and then we observe errors.

[22:22] Rafael Mendes: We can set it NotReady and routing will stop using it. Also we can drain connections gracefully depending on the serving path.

[22:33] Carlos Renteria: 6) Audit logs for override actions.

[22:36] Marcus Lin: Yes, with actor, timestamp, reason; break-glass also triggers alerting.

[22:46] Anika Wolff: Can I ask about communication. Like during an expansion, do we get status updates proactively.

[22:52] Lauren Bishop: For enterprise Dedicated, yes—we can provide a comms plan. Internally we post stage updates; we can mirror a subset to a shared channel or email updates. We’re also adding a bot that posts stage durations and failures.

[23:12] Megan Chu: Email is fine. Slack shared channel is better.

[23:16] Lauren Bishop: Noted.

[23:18] Samir Patel: You mentioned competitors earlier. We’re not against Bedrock, but the performance variability is hard. With Dedicated, the question becomes: are you operationally mature enough that capacity changes don’t become a fire drill.

[23:35] Lauren Bishop: Understood. This automation work is specifically to make it not a fire drill.

[23:43] Megan Chu: I want to hear about paging. Who gets paged if provisioning is stuck.

[23:48] Rafael Mendes: Internally, the owning oncall—infra fleet for provisioning/imaging, platform for control plane registration, and SRE for end-to-end stuckness thresholds. For customer-facing comms, your CSM/eng contact would be looped in.

[24:07] Megan Chu: That’s fine. We just need to know you have an oncall rotation that actually responds.

[24:12] Rafael Mendes: We do.

[24:15] Samir Patel: What about “manual intervention required.” How do you decide.

[24:19] Vanessa Ortiz: If a stage fails with a known remediation (like retryable terraform apply), it will auto-retry. If it fails with a policy block or an unknown error, it stops and escalates.

[24:35] Samir Patel: Okay.

[24:37] Carlos Renteria: One more security question: do you store prompts from perf-canary. Are those customer data.

[24:44] Rina Kobayashi: The readiness suite uses Redwood-owned prompts, generic, not customer data. For customer-specific evals, that’s separate and we can run it in your environment, but readiness gate is generic.

[24:59] Carlos Renteria: Good.

[25:01] Samir Patel: Megan, anything else.

[25:04] Megan Chu: Just one: do you have a definition of “Ready” written down. Like, not marketing language.

[25:10] Lauren Bishop: Yes, we can share it. The short definition: “Ready means the pool is provisioned, bootstrapped, validated, and has passed readiness gates including perf-canary; routing will only send traffic to Ready capacity.” We’ll send the detailed version.

[25:29] Samir Patel: Great.

[25:31] Lauren Bishop: We’re at about halfway. I want to make sure we cover rollout expectations and what you’d need from us for a pilot. Samir, what’s your timeline.

[25:41] Samir Patel: If procurement doesn’t block us, we’d like to pilot next month. But we need internal security sign-off first.

[25:50] Anika Wolff: And we need a clear statement on lead times and what happens if it misses.

[25:56] Lauren Bishop: Understood. We’ll package the SLO proposal and operational boundaries.

[26:03] Carlos Renteria: For security sign-off, we’ll need: SOC2 report, encryption details, access controls, audit logs, image hardening. Probably a session with Marcus.

[26:14] Marcus Lin: Happy to do that. Also we can share our image checklist at a high level—what we pin, what we scan.

[26:24] Megan Chu: I’d also like to see an example of a failure. Like “imaging timed out” and what you do.

[26:31] Vanessa Ortiz: Sure. Common example: imaging times out in a region due to artifact mirror slowness. Our mitigation is fallback to alternate mirror or prewarm caches. The pipeline detects it and either retries or switches sources.

[26:49] Samir Patel: That kind of thing is exactly why we’re asking.

[26:52] Lauren Bishop: Yep.

[26:54] Rina Kobayashi: Another example: perf-canary fails because batching config is wrong. That’s caught in validation and never reaches Ready.

[27:04] Megan Chu: Perfect.

[27:06] Samir Patel: Okay. Let’s talk about the artifacts you’ll send. I want something we can put in front of our CAB.

[27:14] Lauren Bishop: We can send a “readiness evidence pack”: stage breakdown, definition of Ready, sample run report with timestamps, sample perf-canary output, and a note on audit logs/break-glass.

[27:29] Carlos Renteria: Include who has permission to do what.

[27:33] Marcus Lin: Will do—RBAC summary.

[27:36] Megan Chu: And the alerting policy.

[27:39] Rafael Mendes: I’ll include it, yes.

[27:42] Samir Patel: Great.

[27:44] Lauren Bishop: Any concerns about the approach.

[27:47] Samir Patel: Just that you’re still “working toward” the SLO. We need confidence you can meet it.

[27:55] Lauren Bishop: Fair. The reason we’re comfortable discussing it is we have baseline data from prior bring-ups and we’re instrumenting time-to-ready now. We can share what we’ve seen historically plus what we’re targeting.

[28:12] Samir Patel: That would help.

[28:15] Megan Chu: Also, if we end up with Fireworks or something else, it’s because of ops overhead. So the bar is high.

[28:22] Lauren Bishop: Understood.

[28:24] Vanessa Ortiz: For what it’s worth, the automation reduces operator touches and reduces drift. That’s exactly the ops overhead issue.

[28:35] Samir Patel: Okay.

[28:37] Lauren Bishop: Let’s do a quick recap of next steps.

[28:41] Lauren Bishop: I will send a one-pager stage breakdown with p50/p95 targets and definitions. Vanessa will send a sample stage timeline view and failure examples. Rafael will send alerting thresholds and paging policy. Rina will send sample perf-canary JSON output and thresholds. Marcus will confirm image signing/provenance + audit logs detail. Samir and Carlos, you’ll send your CAB/audit requirements and target regions/SKUs.

[29:17] Samir Patel: Yep.

[29:18] Carlos Renteria: Works.

[29:20] Megan Chu: Yes.

[29:22] Anika Wolff: Yes, but please also include commercial language around what’s included in the SLO and what’s out of scope.

[29:29] Lauren Bishop: Noted, I’ll coordinate with our team.
